subject: Communication
title: Erin Meyer's Culture Map
description: A micro-lesson that makes Erin Meyer's Culture Map usable.

hook.text: Erin Meyer mapped eight dimensions where cultures diverge — and showed why your international meeting keeps going wrong.

buildup.text: Her Culture Map plots countries across: Communicating, Evaluating, Persuading, Leading, Deciding, Trusting.

discovery.text: Americans are low-context communicators but relationship-based trusters.

twist.text: A country can be direct in communication but indirect in criticism.

climax.text: Meyer's model is more practical than Hofstede's for business — it maps specific workplace behaviors, not abstract values.

punchline.text: Don't stereotype cultures. Map them. Then adapt.

quiz.question: How many dimensions does Erin Meyer's Culture Map include?

details.summary: Erin Meyer's Culture Map plots cultures along eight behavioral scales including communicating, evaluating, leading, deciding, trusting, disagreeing, scheduling, and persuading. It provides a practical visual tool for comparing any two cultures and predicting friction points.
details.whyItMatters: The Culture Map is the most practical modern framework for global business communication, used by executives worldwide to navigate cultural differences.
takeaways: Eight scales map key business communication behaviors
Relative position between cultures matters more than absolutes
It helps predict specific friction points between any two cultures

faq.question: How is Erin Meyer's model different from Hofstede's?
faq.answer: Meyer's model is designed specifically for business communication and uses eight practical scales rather than abstract dimensions. It emphasizes relative positioning between cultures rather than absolute scores. It is also more recent, drawing on contemporary global business research.

faq.question: Which of the eight scales causes the most business friction?
faq.answer: The communicating scale, measuring low-context versus high-context, and the evaluating scale, measuring direct versus indirect negative feedback, cause the most everyday friction. A Dutch manager giving direct criticism to a Japanese team member often fails despite good intentions.
